thesis: This episode argues that Tencent's WeChat ecosystem is superior because it fulfills consumer needs and provides a frictionless experience with integrated payments, whereas other companies like Grab, Uber, and DoorDash struggle with monetization, retention, and differentiation due to promo wars and a lack of unique value. The discussion highlights that simply stuffing features into an app or offering a frictionless experience alone won't drive switching without addressing fundamental consumer preferences and business model flaws.

claims.claim: WeChat is the dominant app in China, more so than iOS, with immense consumer law that others try to duplicate.
claims.quote: I mean, Wii chat is the dominant app more so than iOS, I would say, in China. I don't know, that's a fair statement, but their law on the consumer is so immense that other people saw that and they say, okay, how do we duplicate that?

claims.claim: Grab does not monetize particularly well and has retention issues due to promo wars and lack of differentiation.
claims.quote: And so if you look at someone like Grab, which was originally ride hailing or Uber, who also recently touted becoming a super app, what they're trying to solve for is a couple things. One, they, they don't monetize particularly well. I know that might be a little contentious, but you could just look at their profitability. They're not really got profitable, right, just on that core offering.

claims.claim: Uber has retention issues and profitability is driven down by promo wars because its offering is not viewed as being very differentiated.
claims.quote: Secondly, is they have retention issues, right? And so maybe Uber's doing this a little bit less so now, but there still are a lot of these sort of promo wars where even having as little as two players in a market is enough that they're driving the profitability of their service down considerably. And so that is kind of a result of the fact that their offering is not viewed as being very different

claims.claim: Users are unwilling to overcome friction to use DoorDash if another service is cheaper or has a restaurant the other doesn't have.
claims.quote: Again, though, in practice, this is not much of a friction that users are unwilling to overcome should they feel like the other service is a little bit cheaper or has a restaurant that one of them doesn't have. And so it's not really a very strong preference that is being filled filled if we're thinking about the consumer higher preferences.

claims.claim: WeChat's early success with mini programs was due to an undeveloped app ecosystem and high mobile usage penetration.
claims.quote: And so the only reason why this was successful, though, was because because this was so early that that the app ecosystem wasn't that developed. Secondarily, because mobile usage penetration exceeded desktop usage, there was much more of a virtue in having a mobile app, a mini program rather than having a website.

claims.claim: WeChat Pay had very high adoption because it was all in the app, allowing seamless creation and rollout of social features.
claims.quote: When they would roll out WeChat Pay, they had very high adoption because, again, it's all in the app. They could create it seamlessly. They could roll out social features and just push it out across everyone who is already in this app and in the social graph.

claims.claim: Tencent was one of the second largest bidders for WhatsApp against Meta, looking at it as an opportunity to do the same thing they did with WeChat globally.
claims.quote: And interestingly enough, the only other very big bidder for WhatsApp, or I guess Google was as well, but Tencent was one of the second largest bidders for WhatsApp against Meta. And so you can imagine they were looking at WhatsApp as sort of an opportunity to do the same thing they did with WeChat globally.

claims.claim: The speaker is skeptical about Meta's ability to replicate Tencent's success with super apps, noting that Meta is stuffing features into WhatsApp but that frictionless experience alone won't drive switching.
claims.quote: And so a super app is something where first is meeting an unmet preference. So it's getting the sale, which could be, you know, just having a mini program on there, having a mobile payment option, whatever it is, that is first just getting the sale initially.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Grab as a tricky one because while they show some success with their super app initiative, it is muddled and not clear that housing everything in an app is the key factor.
claims.quote: Yeah. So Grab's a tricky one because they can show that they've had some success with their super app initiative. And it's a little muddled, right? It's not clear that it's anything of the fact that everything is housed within an app.

claims.claim: Apple's Clips feature was a mini program that wasn't housed in a specific app, but it never became popular because no one found it.
claims.quote: Apple actually did roll out something called clips, which was the idea that it would be a mini program on your phone, except it wasn't housed in any specific app. And so it was something that would appear and then disappear. But then that also meant no one ever found it.

claims.claim: Maituan (Meituan) fulfilled a consumer need and built a better service by serving unmet needs in hotel bookings.
claims.quote: Well, I want to give a little credence to Maitwan. They definitely is nowhere near as good of a business as, as 10 cents as we chat is. But the thing that they did was they did was they did end up fulfilling a consumer need and were able to build a service that is better than it should have been otherwise.

claims.claim: RAB's super app attempt focuses on getting all stuff in the same app, which consumers don't care about since they can just click on a different app.
claims.quote: Whereas when you see a company like RAB go out and try to sell or Uber go out and try to sell their super app, they focus on the point that you could get all of this stuff in the same app. No one really cares about that because they can just go click on a different app.

claims.claim: Elon Musk's X talks about wanting to be a super app, but it's solving a business problem rather than a consumer preference.
claims.quote: And you see this to an extent with, you know, Elon Musk talking about X. He talks about it wanting to be a super app. He talks about all the features they want to have in it. And a lot of the stuff is stuff that already exist or all of it is already existing elsewhere. And it's not that it's solving a consumer's preference. It's that he has a business problem he's trying to solve for.

claims.claim: Twitter is a tough avenue to launch super apps because users want to be anonymous and don't want to tie payment info to it.
claims.quote: And the caveat that is two things. One, you need real identity. And two, you're going to need payment info. And the habits and the way most people use Twitter are they want to be anonymous and they definitely do not want to tie any payment info to that because they want to be anonymous.
